storm.summary_layperson: No storm risk this evening — skies are clear, there's zero instability in the atmosphere, and radar shows nothing on the approach to the cove.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The air-water gap was already down to 4°F by 4 PM, below the ~5°F buffer the marine layer needs, and it keeps sliding to roughly -2°F by 8 PM — there's no protective layer standing tonight, though with no storms around it isn't needed.
storm.detail_html:
Regionally quiet: 0 J/kg CAPE, no NWS watches or warnings, and KOKX radar shows no echoes anywhere near the cove as of the 7:45 PM scan. The NWS forecast for the period calls for "Mostly Sunny" skies, consistent with the flat instability numbers.

The Sound's usual protective marine layer isn't a factor tonight one way or the other. The air-water temperature gap was only 4°F at 4 PM — already under the ~5°F threshold where the layer does meaningful work — and it keeps eroding as the afternoon air cools, going slightly negative (around -2°F) by 8 PM. In a normal year this would matter for storms arriving late; tonight there's nothing inbound for it to blunt.

Bottom line: this is as low-risk an evening as the data supports. The cove and the surrounding towns are in the same boat — clear and stable.

What would change the call: any surprise pop-up convection developing after dark, or a bump in CAPE on a later model cycle. Neither is showing in the current data.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light gradient wind out of the S/SSW around 6-8 kt holds through the window with no sea breeze in play — deltaT is only 4°F, well under the 5°F gate. Pressure is fairly even across the cove with a slight edge toward the mouth and east shore; good light-air racing but watch for the wind going soft and variable after sunset.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a gradient-only, no-sea-breeze evening. The two-ingredient sea-breeze test needs both a deltaT of at least 5°F and a favorable gradient; today's air-water differential is only 4°F (below gate) and the sea-breeze coastal fraction sits at 0.63 — present in the westerly stations but not strong enough on its own to call this a thermal day. Gradient wind (`mean_speed_authoritative_kt`) is 7.9 kt, just under the 8 kt cut for light vs. moderate, so this is a light gradient day (B-light).

Direction is steady out of the S, 179-195° through the window, essentially matching RYC's current read of 192° SSW at 7.1 kt (gusting 7.9). The wider station ensemble runs a touch more veered at 212° median (west-zone median 221° SW), about 20-30° off HRRR/RYC — not a large enough gap to flag a local eddy (direction agreement is 0.74, above the 0.7 threshold), just typical along-coast spread.

Because this is a gradient day, not a thermal one, sunset at 7:01 PM doesn't collapse the wind the way it would on a pure sea-breeze day — the gradient flow doesn't care about the sun. Expect it to hold its general strength and direction through the evening, with the light-air caveat that B-light regimes can go soft and directionally unstable once the boundary layer stabilizes after dark.

With S/SSW flow the cove geography table calls this fairly uniform pressure, maybe a touch stronger near the mouth and along the east shore (less shelter from Tod's Point on this axis). No persistent frontal shift or backdoor risk in play — deltaT doesn't clear the backdoor trigger's own 5°F hot-day gate, and the sentinel stations (KBOS/KPVD/KGON) are all still SW, not flipped NE.

Racers will feel 6-8 kt most of the window — the sweet spot for one-design dinghies, but on the lighter, finickier end of that band. HRRR's direct model output only extends to 8:00 PM local; the 9:00 and 10:00 PM rows are extrapolated from the established trend, not fresh model data, so treat the tail end of the window as lower-confidence.
